tool.second: %TEMP%\combat-mark-native\probe2 (MarkProbe2) for addresses that only appear inside a GenericInstMethod comment
method: dump.cs supplies RVA -> method entry and per-type field offsets; GameAssembly.dll supplies the bytes; Iced x64 decodes each body in place.
A body's range is the next distinct RVA of the same declaring type (cap 0x8000); a tail jump outside that range is listed and decoding continues, so a call after the jump is still visible.
A linear sweep of the whole own range lists every literal call/jump target with its site, separately from the decoded body, because it can invent an edge where data sits inside the range.
Field names come from the declaring type's own `// 0xN` field table in dump.cs.
Nothing is loaded into a process and no game code runs.

methods: public bool TryGet(out EnemyAgent comp)  // RVA 0x19349A0
pTagEnemy.reading: the action's payload is a replicated agent reference, which is what makes the tag itself networked: the marker is not placed by a Forge transport.

duration.reason: no duration parameter reaches PlaceCustomMarker: SyncPlaceNavMarkerTag passes the enemy block's own destroy-delay float (EnemyBalancingData +0x68) and the caller of WantToTagEnemy cannot set it. The catalog's `duration` input therefore has no native destination.
duration.also: PlaceCustomMarker's body decodes 1184 bytes whose only register consumers are PrepareMarker, SetVisualStates, SetTitle(name), the NavMarkerOption bit test and the Component factory; the r9 destroyDelay parameter and its [rsp+20h] stack slot are stored and never read, so the marker is not even reported to fade on that number. EnemyTaggedTimer is a separate comparison value, not a deadline this action can set.

marker.reason: the style is the literal NavMarkerOption.Enemy (0x80) inside SyncPlaceNavMarkerTag; no marker resource, icon or prefab parameter exists on the path.

viewers.reason: the audience is decided by the game's own action replication (SNet_AuthorativeAction<pTagEnemy>), not by the caller; there is no per-viewer parameter at any point of the chain.

recipients.reason: WantToTagEnemy takes exactly one EnemyAgent and packs one pEnemyAgent; a many-target action must submit one call per target.

nonEnemyTargets.reason: the payload type is pEnemyAgent and the placement lives on EnemyAgent; a player, a map object or any other kind has no tag entry point.

why: it is the vanilla entry point (the scan tool's two bodies are its only callers), so the tag it produces is the game's tag with the game's own marker, audience and cleanup;
it takes the native agent directly, so no `pEnemyAgent` value has to be built on this side;
it hands the request to the game's own action system, which is what replicates it; the mod does not need a second transport and must not pretend the placement is local-only.
the alternative, calling EnemyAgent.SyncPlaceNavMarkerTag directly, would place the marker on this machine only: the placement method is not the networked one. It is therefore not used.

authority.evidence: Ask @0x1C26D10 returns before dispatch when SNet.IsMaster is false (0x1C26DC5 -> 0x1C26F01) and before the packet-processor read when the client flag is false (0x1C26E41 -> 0x1C26EEC); the package additionally requires the host's own readiness flag and a `Ready` startup state.
authority.multiplayer: NOT GAME-VERIFIED. What is proven here is static: the payload is a replicated agent reference and the dispatch is the game's own authoritative action, so the tag is the game's own networked tag. Whether a joiner really sees the marker, what it looks like in a replay, and what happens on a host migration were not observed and are not claimed.

handler.body: CombatMarkAdapter.Handle(adapter, context) in ForgeWeapon/Native/CombatMarkAdapter.cs, reached through the adapter's own bound Handle(context) method group
handler.registration: ModuleDefinition.Create(mark) declares the `forge.action.combat.mark` capability row, the `forge.module.gtfo.weapon.binding.mark` execute binding, the handler's shape and its support row only when the native half hands the handler over; EquipmentIdentitySession receives it as its optional `markHandler` and WeaponNativeSession builds the adapter before that registration.
handler.declaredPorts: the catalog's own ports, with the three inputs the native path cannot carry (viewers, marker, duration) and the marker_handle output declared optional: a required input is one a plan must wire, so declaring them required would make every mark step unloadable, and the handler refuses each of them by name when a plan supplies one anyway.
handler.tests: tests/CombatMark covers the request check (RequestCode, including the visibility policy), the per-target chain (Mark), the game index lookup (NativeEnemy), the row shaping (Rows) and the command conclusion (Aggregate); no case is dispatched through a plan end to end, which needs the game's own host.

enemyLookup.decision: CombatMarkAdapter.NativeEnemy parses the canonical decimal id after `gtfo.enemy:` and asks the game's own index, Agents.AgentManager.GetAgent(int gid, out Agent), then TryCasts to EnemyAgent.
why: the kernel's entity tables are one-way — RuntimeKernel.ResolveEntityInstance(kind, instance) maps a native object to the reference its owner allocated and there is no reverse call; the per-kind EntityInstanceResolvers registrations are registry-internal and are not reachable from another provider.
ForgeEnemy owns `gtfo.enemy` and this batch may not modify it, so the hand-off the previous batch assumed (a delegate handed over by the enemy domain) does not exist at runtime.

the enemy domain therefore stays the identity authority anyway: Mark() re-checks the answer with RuntimeKernel.ResolveEntityInstance("gtfo.enemy", agent) == target before any native call, and a disagreement is refused with `mark-identity-mismatch`. A wrong or ambiguous index answer can only make the action refuse, never tag a different enemy.
the id text is parsed with the same canonical-decimal rule the gear-block parser uses: any other spelling answers null instead of being normalized into an id.
enemyLookup.evidence: dump.cs Agents.AgentManager (RVA 0x1929110 GetAgent(int gid, out Agent agent), 0x1929290 InternalGetAgent(int gid)) and Agents.Agent.GlobalID (ushort, the value EnemyModule spells into `gtfo.enemy:<id>`). Static, metadata level only.
enemyLookup.REVIEW: NOT GAME-VERIFIED: that AgentManager.GetAgent is keyed by the same global id the enemy domain spells into its reference was not observed in a running game. If it is not, every mark refuses (the feature does nothing) — it cannot mis-tag. This is the one decision in this batch that most needs a game check.
enemyLookup.rejectedAlternatively: building a second Weapon-side enemy table, guessing a GlobalID without the kernel check, or reading AgentManager without the enemy domain's own resolution agreeing.

remaining: The tag is submitted per target; the game's own tag has no duration, marker resource, viewer list or single-viewer policy, and each of those requests is refused by name (duration-unsupported, marker-unsupported, viewers-unsupported, visibility-unsupported).
In-game verification (multiplayer replication, marker lifetime, BioTracker equivalence) is unchanged and still pending.
